newsitem.title: UK: Reuters/NOP poll -- British at best tepid on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Reuters/NOP poll -- British at best tepid on EMU.

text.p: British voters would prefer to wait and see on European monetary union rather than plunging in at the start of a single currency in 1999, an exclusive Reuters/NOP opinion poll showed on Tuesday.
The survey, which polled 1,049 people around Britain last week, found 41 percent wanted Britain to see how the proposed single currency worked in action before deciding whether to join.
Some 30 percent said the country should stay out altogether.
The poll, conducted on February 21 in 51 parliamentary constituencies, tested what the public thought would happen to the British economy if the country joined, delayed entry or steered clear of EMU.

Analysts said the results reflected widespread public confusion over the issues, echoing messages -- from circumspect to hostile -- coming from both major political parties on the merits or otherwise of the European project.

While both the Conservatives and Labour have pledged to hold a referendum on the single currency, the Referendum Party of tycoon Sir James Goldsmith believes the public is so gripped by the issue that it is fighting the imminent election on that alone.
The poll gave the opposition Labour party a commanding lead over the Conservatives ahead of Britain's election, which must be held by May 22 but is widely tipped to happen on May 1.
Fifty percent of those expressing a voting intention said they would choose Labour and 30 percent the Conservatives. The Referendum Party would take just two percent of the vote.

"The public still seems to be reluctant about currency union, but there is a lot of public confusion about what the party positions are," said Sydney Elliot, senior lecturer in politics at Queen's University in Belfast.

Voters found little to distinguish between the two parties in general on Europe -- 34 percent thought the opposition Labour party was better trusted to represent Britain's interests there, while 31 percent thought the Conservatives were a safer pair of hands.

Although, when added together, a clear majority of respondents, 58 percent, thought Britain should either delay joining or not join a single currency, 38 percent thought that if the project went ahead without Britain the economy would suffer.
Only 14 percent though Britain would be better off economically outside the EMU club.

Opinions were evenly divided over the kind of economic role Britain should have in Europe -- 32 percent said the economy would benefit from closer ties but the same number said a looser relationship would be better.
Another 30 percent thought Britain should keep its current economic relations with Europe the same as they are now.

Prime Minister John Major has been battling to keep his party together on EMU membership but the rifts were exposed again last week when "Eurosceptic" Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said the government was on balance hostile to a single currency.

The Labour party is also committed to a referendum and economics spokesman Gordon Brown has pledged to test the effects of EMU on Britain's jobs, financial services industry and investment climate before committing to entry.
